bibliography.abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.
bibliography.comment: Accepted for publication in International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences, and Applications (ACDSA 2027)
bibliography.title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting

en.caveats: The method serves as an internal auditing tool to prioritize locations for further study rather than providing conclusive proof of crime underreporting.
en.what: The authors developed a self-supervised urban representation learning framework to detect abnormal crime reporting patterns by comparing localized reporting profiles against representation-similar urban peers using only spatial crime records. Evaluating the method on over 1.8 million crime incidents across 1,058 H3 spatial cells in Mexico City, the model achieved a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, outperforming Hex2Vec at 0.2863. The resulting Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) metric maintained high ranking stability across varying neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlation coefficients ranging from 0.9720 to 0.9951.
en.why: This approach allows urban analysts to audit spatial crime data for systematic reporting anomalies and potential spatial distortions without requiring external socioeconomic covariates.
